newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan steps up efforts to woo foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Jordan steps up efforts to woo foreign investors.

text.p: Jordan plans to step up efforts to open its economy to foreign investors and attract funds it fears it is losing to regional rivals, officials said on Monday.
They are concerned Jordan is losing out to countries such as Egypt, Morocco and Lebanon which have seen capital inflows reach new levels over the last year.

"Our priority is improving the investment climate to encourage foreign investment," Jawad al Anani, Deputy Prime Minister for Development Affairs, told Reuters. "We are serious about removing hurdles hampering investments."

Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali's cabinet, appointed in March, has in its first few weeks revived plans to develop a major free-trade zone in the south, widen foreign investment and share ownership in Jordan, and tackle the red tape which turns potential businesses away.

Officials hope the moves will create badly needed jobs and raise living conditions for society's poorer members. That could stem widespread disenchantment among ordinary Jordanians and businesses alike over disappointing gains so far from Jordan's peace treaty with Israel in 1994.
"Yes, foreign investment has been limited...Some of it has come but did not find the right climate and went away. I think we can bring it back," Anani said.
The proposals, some of which have already taken shape and should be implemented soon, would extend concessions under a 1995 investment law to attract Western multinationals.
They may allow the cabinet powers to extend special investment breaks beyond those designated, in order to attract major projects.
The government is also reviving longstanding plans to transform the Red Sea port of Aqaba into a free-trade zone within a year.

It is considering waiving a 50 percent ceiling for foreigners on stock ownership, which hampers fund buying, and a similar restriction on direct investment in sectors such as mining and agriculture, officials say.
"There is a study...and we are inclined even to eliminate some ceilings in some sectors to allow much wider scope and freedom in investment," Anani said.
The changes considered include relaxing restrictions on foreign investment in small service oriented ventures.
Plans include reforms to a cumbersome licensing process by forming a top ministerial committee to ensure rapid approvals.
"What is needed is activating the existing mechanism and taking speedy decisions to avoid the snags and adminstrative hurdles which stand in the way," Anani said.
Critics says projects take on average six months to proceed with investors chasing scores of state bodies from intelligence to local government departments before securing licenses.
